Hi Dad,

Here is what happened in AI today. Each item links to the full story, with plain-language explanations of anything unfamiliar. The links go to a website built especially for you, with a new edition every day, so do check it out.

Question of the day: How does a phone recognise a plant from a photograph? You point the camera at a flower by the path and a second later the phone tells you its name. Sometimes it is right, sometimes it is confidently wrong. The answer is at the end of this email.

  • Britain begins the world’s largest trial of AI in breast cancer screening. Britain’s health service has begun the world’s largest trial of AI in breast cancer screening: about 660,000 to 700,000 women at 30 centres. Today two specialist doctors look at every breast X-ray; the trial will test whether an AI program can safely do part of that work, with at least one doctor still looking at every picture and making the decision. Whether it actually finds more cancers is not yet known; that is what the trial is meant to find out, and it will take years. Read more and the background.
  • Google says teams of AI agents made programs for future quantum computers many times cheaper, with every step checked by machine. Google’s AI laboratory says teams of AI programs, working together and “meeting” every four hours to compare ideas, found much cheaper ways to do several calculations on future quantum computers, including one for fusion energy research that became almost twelve times cheaper. Because those computers do not yet exist, every improvement had to be proved mathematically, and a separate program checked each proof. The figures are Google’s own, and even the improved calculations are still too big for the first quantum computers. Read more and the background.
  • Two US states sue Elon Musk’s companies over sexual images made by the Grok AI. Virginia and Oregon have become the first US states to sue Elon Musk’s companies over Grok, the AI built into the social network X. They say it was released without the usual protections, so that users could make fake sexual pictures of real people, including children, while the company told the public its products were safe. The company says it punishes users who break its rules and reports them to the police. These are accusations so far; the courts will decide. Read more and the background.
  • OpenAI and Cisco release a free tool to shield running computers while a security hole waits to be fixed. AI now finds security holes in software faster than people can repair them. OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, and the network company Cisco have released a free tool that puts up a temporary “shield” on a running computer: it blocks the one action an attacker would need while the real repair is being prepared, without switching anything off. In the companies’ own demonstration, an AI wrote such a shield and it stopped an attack. There is no independent test yet. Read more and the background.

Also on the website today: Riemann hypothesis proof: the strictest check passes, and its author admits “stupid things” in how he announced it, Report: staff at OpenAI and Anthropic doubt their newest unreleased AI can be kept under control, An OpenAI researcher’s advice to gifted students: leave university and join an AI laboratory now.

Answer to the question of the day. It compares your picture with millions of pictures that people have already named. An article in the Russian magazine Sistemny Blok explains it with the example of iNaturalist, a kind of social network for nature lovers: people upload photographs of what they find, and experts say which species it is. At the time of the article (2020) the site held nearly 11 million photographs of plants identified this way. Those labelled pictures are the textbook from which a neural network learns: it is shown a photo together with the right answer, again and again, until it picks up which features go with which species. When you upload a new photo, it is analysed and compared with what the network has already seen. That also explains the mistakes. Common plants have tens of thousands of photographs from all over the world, and the network usually gets them right. But for a great many species there are fewer than five photographs, because the plant is rare, grows somewhere hard to reach, or is hard to tell apart even for specialists. With so little to learn from, the network guesses badly. The background gets in the way too: sky, stones, somebody’s hand, or other grass that the plant almost melts into. And if the picture is blurred and shows only a piece of the flower, as the article puts it, even an experienced professor might not name it. So a wrong answer does not mean the app is bad; it means that for this plant the network has not yet seen enough examples. The same rule holds for much of today’s AI: it knows well what it has seen often. Sistemny Blok, “How a neural network recognises plants and why it gets them wrong” (article in Russian).
